title: Redis Persistence
subtitle: RDB snapshots vs AOF and hybrid persistence
author: KERNAL

whyItExists.problem: Redis stores data in RAM. Without persistence, every restart means complete data loss — unacceptable for session stores, queues, and any data you can't afford to lose.
whyItExists.solution: Redis offers two persistence mechanisms: RDB (periodic snapshots to disk) and AOF (append-only log of every write). Each has different durability and performance tradeoffs. Hybrid mode combines both.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Any Redis that holds data you cannot rebuild on restart: sessions, queues, rate limit counters, Streams. Even pure caches benefit from persistence to warm up faster after restart.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: If Redis is used exclusively as an ephemeral cache with a cold-start warm-up acceptable, you can disable persistence to squeeze extra performance.

explainModes.beginner: RDB is like taking a photo of your data every few minutes. AOF is like writing down every change you make in a diary. If something goes wrong, you restore from the last photo (RDB) or replay the diary (AOF).
explainModes.simple: RDB saves a snapshot of all data to disk periodically. Fast startup, may lose last few minutes of writes. AOF logs every write command. Almost zero data loss, slower startup. Hybrid does both: fast startup + good durability.
explainModes.standard: RDB uses fork() to create a child process that writes a compact binary snapshot. The parent continues serving requests. AOF appends each write command as text. On startup, Redis replays the AOF to restore state. Hybrid (aof-use-rdb-preamble) writes an RDB preamble at AOF rewrite time, combining fast load with low data loss.
explainModes.technical: RDB fork uses copy-on-write semantics — the parent and child share memory pages until the parent writes, triggering a page copy. Memory spikes during save proportional to write rate. AOF fsync policies: always (1 write/command, safest), everysec (1 fsync/sec, default), no (OS decides). AOF rewrite compacts the log by writing current state without historical commands.
explainModes.deepDive: Redis 7.0 introduced Multi-Part AOF (MP-AOF) to eliminate the atomic rename needed at rewrite time. The AOF is split into a base file (the last RDB preamble) and incremental files. This reduces fsync pauses and disk space during rewrite. The aof_manifest file tracks the parts. On load, Redis replays base + incrementals in order. For minimum data loss in a cluster, enable AOF with everysec on all replicas too.

content.text: Redis stores everything in RAM. Without persistence, a server restart, power failure, or crash means total data loss. Redis provides two persistence mechanisms with different tradeoffs between durability and performance.
RDB creates a point-in-time snapshot of all data. Redis forks a child process to write the snapshot — the parent keeps serving requests with minimal impact.

content.code:
# redis.conf — RDB configuration

# Save rules: save <seconds> <changes>
# Save if at least 1 change happened in 3600 seconds
save 3600 1
# Save if at least 100 changes happened in 300 seconds
save 300 100
# Save if at least 10000 changes happened in 60 seconds
save 60 10000

# RDB filename and directory
dbfilename dump.rdb
dir /var/lib/redis

# Compress RDB (uses LZF compression)
rdbcompression yes

# Manual save (blocks server — don't use in production)
# redis-cli SAVE

# Non-blocking save
# redis-cli BGSAVE

# Check last save time
# redis-cli LASTSAVE

content.definition: Redis Database — a compact binary snapshot of all data at a point in time. Fast to load on restart but may lose up to minutes of writes if Redis crashes between saves.

content.text: AOF logs every write command. On restart, Redis replays all commands to reconstruct the dataset. It provides much better durability — typically less than 1 second of data loss.

content.code:
# redis.conf — AOF configuration
appendonly yes
appendfilename "appendonly.aof"

# Fsync policy (how often to flush to disk)
# always   — fsync after every write (safest, slowest)
# everysec — fsync once per second (recommended default)
# no       — let OS decide (fastest, least safe)
appendfsync everysec

# Rewrite AOF to compact it (removes historical commands)
auto-aof-rewrite-percentage 100  # rewrite when AOF doubles in size
auto-aof-rewrite-min-size 64mb   # only if AOF is at least 64MB

# Trigger manual AOF rewrite (non-blocking)
# redis-cli BGREWRITEAOF

content.definition: Append-Only File — a log of every write command in RESP format. Near-zero data loss with everysec fsync (up to 1 second loss), but slower startup and larger files than RDB.

content.text: Hybrid persistence combines the fast startup of RDB with the low data loss of AOF. At AOF rewrite time, Redis writes an RDB preamble, then appends subsequent commands. On restart it loads the RDB preamble (fast) then replays only the new AOF tail (small).

content.code:
# redis.conf — Recommended production setup
appendonly yes
appendfsync everysec
aof-use-rdb-preamble yes   # hybrid mode: RDB preamble + AOF tail

auto-aof-rewrite-percentage 100
auto-aof-rewrite-min-size 64mb

# Save RDB as backup too
save 3600 1
save 300 100

a.name: RDB
weaknesses: Fork can spike memory under heavy write load
a.useWhen: Backup, disaster recovery, tolerable data loss window

b.name: AOF
strengths: Up to 1-second data loss with everysec
b.useWhen: Session stores, queues, any data with strict durability requirements

content.text: For most production Redis deployments, enable hybrid persistence: appendonly yes + aof-use-rdb-preamble yes + appendfsync everysec. This gives fast startup and at most 1 second of data loss.
RDB fork() can temporarily double memory usage under a heavy write load due to copy-on-write. Set maxmemory to no more than 50% of RAM if RDB saves are frequent.

questions.question: Which persistence mode has the least data loss?
questions.explanation: AOF with always fsync writes to disk on every command — zero data loss but slowest. everysec risks up to 1 second of writes. RDB can lose minutes.

questions.question: What is hybrid persistence in Redis?
options: Using both a primary and replica
Using RDB and AOF files in separate directories
AOF with an RDB preamble: fast startup + low data loss
Storing some data in RAM and some on disk
questions.explanation: Hybrid (aof-use-rdb-preamble yes) writes an RDB snapshot as the AOF preamble at rewrite time. On startup, Redis loads the compact RDB then replays only the smaller AOF tail — fast load with low data loss.

questions.question: Why can RDB saves temporarily double Redis memory?
options: Redis copies all data before saving
Fork creates a child process sharing memory via copy-on-write; writes cause page duplication
RDB compresses data which requires extra space
questions.explanation: RDB uses fork(). The child process shares memory pages with the parent via copy-on-write. Each write in the parent triggers a page copy, potentially doubling memory if write rate is high during the save.

faq.q: Can I use both RDB and AOF?
faq.a: Yes. The recommended setup is hybrid persistence: AOF with an RDB preamble (aof-use-rdb-preamble yes). This gives fast startup from the RDB portion and minimal data loss from the AOF tail.

faq.q: How do I disable persistence for a pure cache?
faq.a: Set 'save ""' (empty string) in redis.conf to disable RDB, and appendonly no to disable AOF. The instance becomes volatile — all data is lost on restart.

faq.q: How large will the AOF file get?
faq.a: It grows with every write until a rewrite compacts it. Redis triggers auto-rewrite when the AOF doubles in size (auto-aof-rewrite-percentage 100). Force a rewrite with BGREWRITEAOF.

usedIn: primary data stores on managed Redis (ElastiCache, Redis Cloud)
examples: Using hybrid AOF (aof-use-rdb-preamble yes) for a session store that must survive instance restarts
Disabling persistence entirely for a pure page-cache layer where a cold start is acceptable
